specPoints.text: describe the reactions of hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid and nitric acid with metals, bases and metal carbonates (excluding the reactions between nitric acid and metals) to form salts

primer.text: From Acids, Bases & Salt Preparations you know the solubility rules and the proton picture of acids and bases. This note catalogues the three great acid reaction families: with metals above hydrogen, with bases, and with metal carbonates. Each family has its own products, its own equations, and one unmistakable sign, the fizzing of carbonate reactions.

lessons.title: Reactions of acids with metals
lessons.opening: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids, and the more reactive the metal, the more vigorous the reaction. Potassium and sodium react dangerously fast, so they are never used in school glassware. In every such reaction the products are a salt and hydrogen gas, summarised as metal + acid giving salt + hydrogen.
keyPoints: A metal must sit above hydrogen in the series to react with dilute acids.
The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with acid.
Potassium and sodium react with acids explosively.
Acid-metal reactions always give a salt and hydrogen.
Sulfuric acid makes sulfate salts and hydrochloric acid makes chloride salts.

low.restatement: The reactivity series is the gate: metals below hydrogen never react with dilute acids, and metals above it react faster the higher they sit. Every successful reaction makes a salt and bubbles of hydrogen.
low.analogy: Think of a queue at a ride with a height bar: below the bar, hydrogen, no entry; above it, the taller the metal, the wilder the ride.
low.examPointer: Expect equation-writing from the summary table: swap the acid to change the salt name, and always add hydrogen as the second product.

medium.restatement: Position above hydrogen is the licence to react, and vigour rises with reactivity, which is why potassium and sodium react explosively and are excluded from classroom acids. The products are systematic: a salt named after the acid, chloride from hydrochloric acid and sulfate from sulfuric acid, plus hydrogen gas, following the general equation metal + acid gives salt + hydrogen.
medium.analogy: Treat the acid as a name-stamp: hydrochloric stamps chlorides and sulfuric stamps sulfates onto whatever metal enters, with hydrogen always released as the by-product.
medium.examPointer: Compare-table questions ask for products at speed, so memorise the acid-to-salt mapping before revising individual equations.

check.stem: Which metals react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid?

options.text: Those above hydrogen in the reactivity series
options.explanation: The series sets the rule: above hydrogen means reaction, below means no reaction.
Copper, silver and gold sit below hydrogen and do not react with dilute acids.
Group 1 metals do react, but explosively; magnesium, zinc and iron react too, more manageably.
That inverts the rule; below hydrogen means no reaction with dilute acids.

check.stem: What are the products when a metal reacts with a dilute acid?

options.explanation: This is the general equation of record: metal + acid gives salt + hydrogen.
Salt plus water is the acid-base pattern; metals give hydrogen instead.

options.text: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: That triple belongs to carbonate reactions, not metals.
No oxide forms; the metal dissolves into the salt while hydrogen bubbles off.

check.stem: Why are potassium and sodium never used with acids in school experiments?

options.text: They react with acids explosively, which is far too dangerous
options.explanation: Their very high reactivity makes the reaction violent, so safer mid-series metals are used instead.

options.text: They do not react with acids at all
options.explanation: They react far too well; danger, not inertness, excludes them.

options.text: They are too rare and expensive
options.explanation: Cost is not the stated reason; the explosive reaction is.
Dissolving metal would itself be reaction; these metals explode instead.

check.stem: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid. Which salt forms?

options.explanation: Sulfuric acid always stamps sulfate onto the metal's name.
Chlorides come from hydrochloric acid, not sulfuric.
Nitrates come from nitric acid.
Carbonates are not products of acid reactions at all; they are reactants.

check.stem: Magnesium, zinc and iron all react with dilute sulfuric acid. Which reacts most slowly?

options.text: Iron, the least reactive of the three
options.explanation: Lower reactivity means a gentler reaction, and iron sits lowest of the trio.
Magnesium reacts fastest, not slowest, because it is highest of the three.

options.text: Zinc, because it is the densest
options.explanation: Density is not the variable; position in the series is.

options.text: All three react at the same speed
options.explanation: The table shows clearly different vigour for each metal.

lessons.title: Acids with bases and metal carbonates
sourceHeadings: Reactions of Acids with Metal Carbonates
lessons.opening: When an acid meets a base, a neutralisation occurs and the products are a salt and water; metal oxides and metal hydroxides both act as bases. With metal carbonates there is a third product: the fizzing of carbon dioxide gas, which makes carbonate reactions unmistakable. In each family the salt name tracks the acid, giving chlorides, sulfates or nitrates.
keyPoints: Acid + base gives salt + water, and the reaction is a neutralisation.
Both metal oxides and metal hydroxides can play the base role.
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates.
Acid + metal carbonate gives salt + carbon dioxide + water.
Effervescence of carbon dioxide marks the carbonate reaction.

low.restatement: Bases mop up acids into salt and water, and carbonates add the fizz of carbon dioxide on top of that pair. Either way the salt's name comes from the acid involved: hydrochloric gives chlorides, sulfuric gives sulfates, and nitric gives nitrates, so naming the salt never requires guessing.
low.analogy: The carbonate reaction is the only one that throws a party, with visible bubbles; the base reaction is the quiet one that just leaves salt and water behind when the guests go home.
low.examPointer: Spot-the-family questions hinge on the products: water present means a base was used, bubbles mean a carbonate, and hydrogen means a metal.

medium.restatement: The base route is neutralisation: metal oxides and hydroxides accept the acid's protons to give a salt and water, with the salt named by the acid, chloride, sulfate or nitrate. The carbonate route adds carbon dioxide, whose effervescence distinguishes it immediately, following the general pattern acid + metal carbonate gives salt + carbon dioxide + water, with nitric acid excluded from the metal family only.
medium.analogy: Picture two recipes sharing the same base ingredients, salt and water, where the carbonate version simply adds a fizzing extra course of carbon dioxide.
medium.examPointer: The exam hint is the giveaway: any acid reaction producing effervescence must involve a metal carbonate making carbon dioxide.

check.stem: What forms when an acid reacts with a metal oxide such as copper(II) oxide?

options.explanation: Metal oxides act as bases, so the neutralisation pattern applies: salt plus water, as in CuO + H2SO4 giving CuSO4 + H2O.
Hydrogen comes from metals; oxides react through the neutralisation pattern.

options.text: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide needs a carbonate; copper(II) oxide contains none.
The copper stays as ions in the salt; no free metal appears.

check.stem: What are the three products when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?

options.text: A salt, carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: This triple defines the carbonate family, complete with visible fizzing of the gas.
That is the metal family's pair; carbonates release carbon dioxide instead.
The carbonate adds its third product, the carbon dioxide gas.
That belongs to blast-furnace chemistry, not acid-carbonate work.

check.stem: Which substances act as bases in these acid reactions?

options.explanation: The note names both families as bases that neutralise acids to salt and water.
Carbonates do react with acids, but they add carbon dioxide; the base pair named is oxides and hydroxides.
Metals give hydrogen, not the salt-and-water pattern of bases.
Acids react with bases; they do not act as them.

check.stem: Nitric acid reacts with zinc oxide. Which salt forms?

options.explanation: Nitric acid produces nitrates, as in ZnO + 2HNO3 giving Zn(NO3)2 + H2O.
Sulfates come from sulfuric acid.
Chlorides come from hydrochloric acid.
Carbonates are reactants in this family, never products.

check.stem: An unknown solid fizzes vigorously when dilute acid is added. What does this reveal?

options.text: The solid is a metal carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Effervescence in an acid reaction is the signature of a carbonate making carbon dioxide gas.

options.text: The solid is a metal oxide, releasing hydrogen
options.explanation: Oxides react quietly to salt and water; the fizz points elsewhere.

options.text: The solid is a metal, releasing oxygen
options.explanation: Metals release hydrogen, and only if they are reactive enough; oxygen never appears here.
Dilute acids are not hot; the bubbles are a chemical product, not boiling.

glossary.definition: The ionic compound made when an acid's hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium partner.
A substance such as a metal oxide or hydroxide that neutralises an acid to salt and water.
The acid-base reaction whose products are a salt and water.
A compound whose acid reaction gives a salt, carbon dioxide and water.
The fizzing caused by a gas escaping from a reaction mixture.
A metal combined with oxygen, which acts as a base in acid reactions.
The salt family produced when hydrochloric acid reacts.
The salt family produced when nitric acid reacts.
